overview: Two large-scale sequencing strategies that trade cost and speed against completeness of genomic coverage.
genZNote: WGS reads the whole book. WES just reads the highlighted chapters (exons).

aspects.label: Overview / Core Definition
aspects.valueA: Sequences essentially the entire genome, including coding and non-coding regions.
aspects.valueB: Sequences only the protein-coding exons of the genome, roughly 1-2% of total DNA.

aspects.label: Coverage Scope
aspects.valueA: Comprehensive — captures coding regions, introns, regulatory regions, and intergenic DNA.
aspects.valueB: Targeted — captures only exons, missing most regulatory and non-coding variants.

aspects.label: Cost and Data Volume
aspects.valueA: Higher cost and larger data storage/analysis burden.
aspects.valueB: Lower cost and smaller, more manageable data volume.

aspects.label: Clinical Diagnostic Yield
aspects.valueA: Can detect structural variants, deep intronic variants, and regulatory region mutations WES would miss.
aspects.valueB: Efficient for finding coding-region mutations responsible for many Mendelian diseases, at lower cost.

aspects.label: Typical Use Case
aspects.valueA: Research applications and cases where exome sequencing has failed to find a causative variant.
aspects.valueB: First-line diagnostic sequencing for suspected genetic disorders with a likely coding-region cause.
